name: crandel
author: clothes-dressing-packing designer
description: Washing hanging on lines, drawn small. CLUE: ONE GROUP PER LINE, separated by "/", e.g. `321/531/2` = three washing lines. Group i is `<rows><longs><drips>`: `rows` = how many rows of air hang under that line (2-6, 8-12 in all, 3 or 4 lines), `longs` = how many garments on that line hang ALL THE WAY DOWN to the line below, `drips` = how many of THOSE hang over a GAP between two garments of the line below - i.e. they are dripping through onto the floor between two things instead of onto the washing. `drips` ranges freely over 0..longs (v2 pinned it to {longs-2, longs-1}, which nearly determined it); generate() only rejects clues where drips == longs on every line, because those cannot be drawn with the v2-reading falsified. The LAST group is a single digit: the bottom line has nothing below it, so it carries only its row count. SOLUTION: an ASCII drying rack, every row the same width (the drawer picks 22-28). A row whose characters are only "=" and "v" is a LINE ("v" = a peg, cosmetic and unchecked); every other row is air. A GARMENT is a horizontal run of one capital letter hanging from the line above: it must appear in the top row of its block and the identical run must repeat down to its hem, so garments are rectangles and each row's runs are a subset of the row above. Everything else - filler char, letters, widths, hems, pegs, how many garments - is free. The scorer rebuilds the clue from the picture (rows per line; long garments per line; how many of those hang over daylight between two garments of the next line) and compares strings. PRIVATE - INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH: one demo gives "washing on lines"; the grammar is rebuilt in 1-2 demos; the FIRST digit of each group is readable straight off the picture (count the rows) and is what tells a solver that a group belongs to a line; the SECOND digit ("how many hang right down to the next line") is the foothold - getting it alone and choosing the drippers at random scores 8.8 %, a real improving signal rather than a wall of zeros; the THIRD digit is the lateral step. v2 counted "of the long ones, how many overlap SOMETHING below", which is the first thing anybody guesses and - fatally - is invisible inside the cheap witness: both Opus players cracked v2 in round 3 with a slot grid of full-height garments in which every refinement of "overlaps" collapses to the same number. v3 counts the opposite kind of landing: the garment is long AND part of it hangs over the daylight BETWEEN two garments underneath, so the water goes past the washing and hits the floor. On a slot grid nothing ever overhangs a gap, so the v2 crack scores 0.0-0.4 % against v3 (measured on both players' round-4 code). The near-misses are alive but bounded: "it has bare floor under it somewhere" (which also counts a garment hung past the END of the line below, where there is floor but no gap) pays 39.5 %, and solve() falsifies it in every demo by always hanging one non-counted long garment past the end. WITNESS TABLE (500 fresh clues; every attacker knows the grammar AND the first two digits, and differs only in the law it uses for the third; each draws in its own naive style): true rule 100 %; "bare floor under part of it" 39.5 %; "not at either end" 16.8 %; "drips onto the same letter" 13.1 %; "wide" 12.4 %; "hangs over two garments" 11.7 %; "fully covers something below" 10.9 %; "in the left half" 9.9 %; "overlaps something below" (THE v2 RULE) 9.8 %; "nothing at all under it" 9.5 %; random among the long ones 8.8 %; "drips onto a garment that is itself long" 8.1 %; "narrow" 6.3 %; "sits entirely over one garment below" 4.4 %; "all the long ones" cannot be built at all. TEMPLATES: identical garment columns on every line 0.0 %; the same with every garment full length 0.0 %; two garments a line 0.0 %; right rows, random hems 0.2 %; previous answer replayed 0.0 %; one fixed answer for every clue 0.2 %; the two v2 crackers' shipped code 0.4 % / 0.0 %; empty/junk/clue echoed 0.0 % (20000 junk strings: 0 raises, 0 non-binary, 0 false positives, worst score() 0.13 ms). ~12000 distinct clue classes (v2 ~6500), so brute-force-and-cache over 6x450 probes is worth ~5-9 % of the final on top of the ~9 % blind rate, i.e. the no-insight ceiling is ~15-18 % (v2 ~26 %). HYPOTHESIS ELIMINATION: over a family of 320 per-line readouts (now including "what is it landing on" and letters), 6.9 survive one demo, 1.2 survive two, and the true rule is the ONLY survivor from demo 3 in 30/30 trials - the demos are informative, the difficulty is generating the hypothesis. v3 (2026-09-04, hardening pass after both Opus players cracked v2 in round 3): drips freed to 0..longs; the counted relation changed from "overlaps something below" to "hangs over a gap between two garments below"; the picture, the clue shape and the legibility work of v2 are unchanged (pegs, daylight beside every garment, 2-6-wide garments, 22-28 columns, one group per line). solve() draws the relation loudly: a counted garment either sits squarely inside the daylight between two garments below or straddles the whole gap with an overhang each side, while a long garment that does NOT count is tucked entirely over one garment below (or hung past the end of the line), and 21 rival per-line readouts are rejected before a picture is shipped. Author: clothes/dressing/packing direction.
